title: Infectious Disease: Malaria, TB and Pandemics
welcome_lead: From an Anopheles mosquito's bite to global pandemic response — study the geography of infectious disease.
meta_desc: Geography Adventure: malaria, TB and pandemic responses including Ebola and COVID-19.
final_note: You have studied diseases in their place. Geography, ecology and health systems all shape outbreaks.

concepts.def: Parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium spp., transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, killing over 600,000 people annually.
Bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transmitted by airborne droplets, killing about 1.3 million people annually.
Epidemic spread over multiple countries or continents, e.g. COVID-19 declared by WHO 11 March 2020.
Living organism, often an arthropod, that transmits pathogens from one host to another.
Indirect protection from infection when a sufficient proportion of a population is immune.
Average number of secondary infections produced by one case in a fully susceptible population.

walkthroughs.body_html: Anopheles mosquitoes thrive in warm, humid climates. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for about 95% of malaria deaths, mostly among children under 5. Interventions — bed nets, indoor spraying, artemisinin-based combinations and the new RTS,S and R21 vaccines — drove substantial reductions before partial reversal during COVID-19 disruptions.

TB is preventable and curable, yet remains one of the world's deadliest infections. Crowded housing, malnutrition and HIV co-infection raise risk. Multi-drug-resistant TB threatens progress; the DOTS strategy and newer drug regimens are central to WHO's End TB Strategy.

The 2014-16 West African Ebola outbreak killed over 11,000 people and exposed weaknesses in global preparedness. COVID-19, declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020, killed an estimated 7 million people directly, with excess mortality far higher. The pandemic accelerated mRNA vaccine technology and global health diplomacy debates.
